Introduction to plot2

Source: vignettes/plot2.Rmd
plot2.Rmd

plot2() creates a complete ggplot2 plot from a single function call. You describe what you want to see, and plot2() determines how to draw it: it chooses the plot type, summarises the data, sorts, sets colours, axes and data labels, and applies a clean theme. The result is an ordinary ggplot object, so everything that ggplot2 offers remains available afterwards.

This vignette introduces the main ideas. It uses the admitted_patients data set that comes with the package, a fictitious set of 250 hospital admissions, and some data sets from base R.

library(plot2)

admitted_patients
#> # A tibble: 250 × 7
#>    date       patient_id gender   age age_group hospital ward   
#>    <date>          <dbl> <chr>  <dbl> <ord>     <fct>    <chr>  
#>  1 2002-01-14          1 M         78 75+       D        Non-ICU
#>  2 2002-03-17          2 M         78 75+       C        Non-ICU
#>  3 2002-04-08          3 M         78 75+       A        ICU    
#>  4 2002-04-14          4 M         72 55-74     C        Non-ICU
#>  5 2002-05-07          5 M         83 75+       C        Non-ICU
#>  6 2002-05-16          6 F         65 55-74     B        ICU    
#>  7 2002-05-16          7 M         47 25-54     D        Non-ICU
#>  8 2002-06-18          8 M         30 25-54     B        ICU    
#>  9 2002-06-23          9 M         82 75+       D        Non-ICU
#> 10 2002-06-23          9 M         82 75+       D        Non-ICU
#> # ℹ 240 more rows

Four directions

Every plot is described by up to four plotting directions, which are also the first four arguments of plot2():

  • x: the values along the x axis;
  • y: the values along the y axis;
  • category: the groups within the plot, shown as colours (in ggplot2 this is the colour or fill aesthetic, depending on the geom);
  • facet: the groups shown in separate panels.

Columns are given without quotes, as in dplyr:

admitted_patients |>
  plot2(x = hospital, y = age, category = gender, facet = ward)
#> Using type = "boxplot" since all groups in hospital and gender and ward contain at least three values
#> Assuming facet.fixed_y = TRUE since the two y scales differ by less than 25%
#> Assuming facet.repeat_labels_y = FALSE since y has fixed scales

Since these are the first four arguments, the names can be left out. The following call gives the same plot:

admitted_patients |>
  plot2(hospital, age, gender, ward)

plot2() fills in what is not given. The iris data have four numeric columns and a factor, so a call without any directions plots the first two numeric columns as points, coloured by the factor:

iris |>
  plot2()
#> Using x = Sepal.Length
#> Using y = Sepal.Width
#> Using category = Species
#> Using type = "point" since both axes are numeric

Each automatic decision follows a fixed rule. In an interactive session, plot2() reports these decisions in a message, such as Using category = Species; set options(plot2.silent = TRUE) to hide them. Any decision is overridden by setting the argument concerned. The section Automatic choices in ?plot2 lists all rules.

Calculations in arguments

The directions accept calculations on the columns of the data. For y, this means that the data are summarised per group, without a separate group_by() and summarise() step:

admitted_patients |>
  plot2(x = hospital, y = n_distinct(patient_id))

Every value of x is now one bar, so plot2() chose a column plot and added data labels. Use y = n() to count rows, or any other function that returns a single value per group, such as mean(), median() or max().

The other directions accept calculations too:

admitted_patients |>
  plot2(x = format(date, "%Y"),
        y = median(age),
        category = ifelse(ward == "ICU", "Intensive care", "Other wards"),
        type = "line")

n() and n_distinct() are re-exported from dplyr, together with the tidyselect helpers such as where() and starts_with(), so they work without loading other packages. A helper can select several columns for y, which are then shown as a category:

iris |>
  plot2(x = Species, y = where(is.double))
#> Using y = c(Petal.Length, Petal.Width, Sepal.Length, Sepal.Width)
#> Using type = "boxplot" since all groups in Species and category contain at least three values

Titles accept calculations as well, which keeps them correct when the data change. glue::glue() also works here:

admitted_patients |>
  plot2(x = age,
        type = "histogram",
        title = paste("Age of", n_distinct(patient_id), "patients"),
        subtitle = paste("Based on", n(), "admissions"),
        caption = paste("Admitted between", min(format(date, "%Y")), "and", max(format(date, "%Y"))))
#> Using binwidth = 6.4 based on data
#> Assuming smooth = TRUE for type = "histogram"

Plot types

Without a type, plot2() chooses one from the data: a boxplot if every group contains at least three values, points if both axes are numeric, and columns otherwise. The type argument sets it explicitly. It accepts the name of any ggplot2 geom, with or without the geom_ prefix, and abbreviations such as "l" for lines and "b" for boxplots:

admitted_patients |>
  plot2(x = hospital, y = age, type = "violin")

plot2() also adds types that ggplot2 does not provide directly, such as dumbbell, back-to-back, Sankey, spider and UpSet plots. A dumbbell plot compares two groups:

admitted_patients |>
  plot2(x = hospital, y = median(age), category = gender, type = "dumbbell")

vignette("supported_types", package = "plot2") shows every type with its data requirements.

Sorting and limiting

Each direction can be sorted with one argument: x.sort, category.sort and facet.sort. They accept TRUE (alphabetical, with numbers in their numeric order), "freq-desc" and "freq-asc" (by the values of y), FALSE (in the order of the data), or a vector with the desired order:

mtcars |>
  plot2(x = carb, y = n(), x.sort = "freq-desc")
#> Using x.character = TRUE since x.sort is set

A vector does not need to contain all values; the remaining values follow in their usual order:

admitted_patients |>
  plot2(x = hospital,
        y = n(),
        category = gender,
        x.sort = c("D", "B"),
        category.sort = "alpha-desc")

x.max_items, category.max_items and facet.max_items limit the number of values shown. The values beyond the limit are combined into one item, which is placed last:

mtcars |>
  plot2(x = carb, y = n(), x.sort = "freq-desc", x.max_items = 4)
#> Using x.character = TRUE since x.sort is set

Stacking

Columns of different categories are placed next to each other. stacked = TRUE stacks them, and stacked_fill = TRUE stacks them to 100%:

admitted_patients |>
  plot2(x = age_group, y = n(), category = hospital, stacked = TRUE)

admitted_patients |>
  plot2(x = age_group, y = n(), category = hospital, stacked_fill = TRUE)

Axes and data labels

All settings of a direction share its name as a prefix, such as x.title, y.limits or category.title. The y axis starts at zero where possible; y.zoom = TRUE (or zoom = TRUE for both axes) limits it to the range of the data. horizontal = TRUE turns the plot, and a type = "bar" gives horizontal columns:

admitted_patients |>
  plot2(x = age_group,
        y = n(),
        category = gender,
        type = "bar",
        x.title = "Age group",
        y.title = "Number of admissions",
        category.title = "Gender")

Axis values can be formatted with functions, such as y.percent = TRUE for percentages or y.labels for any labelling function. A secondary y axis is set with y_secondary. This example uses the economics data set from ggplot2:

ggplot2::economics |>
  plot2(x = date,
        y = unemploy / 1000,
        y_secondary = psavert,
        type = "line",
        colour = "#4E79A7",
        y_secondary.colour = "#F28E2B",
        x.title = NULL,
        y.title = "Unemployed (millions)",
        y_secondary.title = "Personal savings rate (%)")
#> Using x.date_breaks = "5 years" based on data
#> Using x.date_labels = "yyyy" based on data

Data labels are added automatically to column plots with at most 25 values. datalabels = TRUE always shows them, datalabels = FALSE hides them, and datalabels.format sets their text. In this format, %n is the value and %p its percentage:

admitted_patients |>
  plot2(x = hospital, y = n(), datalabels.format = "%n (%p)")

Colours

colour sets the colours for every plot type. In ggplot2, this requires either the colour or the fill aesthetic with its matching scale function, depending on the geom. colour accepts colour names, hexadecimal codes, palette names such as "viridis", and named vectors that match the values of category:

admitted_patients |>
  plot2(x = hospital,
        y = n(),
        category = gender,
        colour = c(F = "#4E79A7", M = "#F28E2B"))

category.focus highlights one value and shows the others in grey:

admitted_patients |>
  plot2(x = format(date, "%Y"),
        y = n(),
        category = hospital,
        category.focus = "B",
        type = "line")

The article Colours and themes on the package website describes palettes, custom organisation colours and themes in more detail.

Adding layers

The add_*() functions add a layer to an existing plot. They use the data of the plot unless other data are given, and they take the category of the plot into account:

p <- mtcars |>
  plot2(x = mpg, y = hp, category = factor(cyl), category.title = "Cylinders")
#> Using type = "point" since both axes are numeric

p |>
  add_line(y = mean(hp), legend.value = "Mean per group")

add_line(), add_point(), add_col(), add_errorbar() and add_smooth() cover the most common layers, and add_type() adds any other geom. A smooth can also be set directly with the smooth argument of plot2():

mtcars |>
  plot2(x = mpg, y = hp, smooth = TRUE, smooth.method = "lm")
#> Using type = "point" since both axes are numeric
#> `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

Other kinds of input

plot2() is an S3 generic. Besides data frames, it plots vectors, tables, formulas, matrices, and models and other objects that ggplot2::fortify() or broom::augment() convert to a data frame. A formula has the form y ~ x + category | facet:

plot2(hp ~ mpg + factor(cyl), data = mtcars)
#> Using type = "point" since both axes are numeric

A correlation matrix becomes a heatmap:

mtcars |>
  cor() |>
  plot2(colour = c("#2166AC", "white", "#B2182B"),
        datalabels = TRUE,
        category.title = "Correlation")
#> Assuming type = "tile" since the matrix contains identical row and column names
#> Using category.midpoint = 0 (the current category scale centre)

A model is converted with broom::augment(), which adds columns such as the fitted values (.fitted) and the residuals (.resid) to the data of the model. This gives a residual plot:

lm(hp ~ mpg, data = mtcars) |>
  plot2(x = .fitted, y = .resid, x.title = "Fitted values", y.title = "Residuals")
#> Using type = "point" since both axes are numeric

Geographic data of class sf become maps; the article Maps on the package website describes them. ?plot2-methods lists all methods.

Continuing with ggplot2

The result of plot2() is a ggplot object. Any ggplot2 layer, scale, coordinate system or theme element can be added with +:

admitted_patients |>
  plot2(x = hospital, y = mean(age), y.title = "Mean age", datalabels = FALSE) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = mean(admitted_patients$age), linetype = "dashed")

By default, plot2() uses theme_minimal2(), a variant of ggplot2::theme_minimal() with fewer lines and more white space. The theme argument sets another theme, and theme = NULL uses the default ggplot2 theme.

Settings for all plots

Package options set defaults for all plots in a session, such as the colours (plot2.colour), the font (plot2.font), the theme (plot2.theme) and the decimal mark (plot2.decimal.mark). Set them with options(), for example in an .Rprofile file:

options(plot2.colour = "viridis",
        plot2.decimal.mark = ",")

?plot2-options lists all options.

Learning more

  • vignette("supported_types", package = "plot2") shows all plot types.
  • ?plot2 documents every argument. Its section Automatic choices describes how missing arguments are determined.
  • The package website, https://msberends.github.io/plot2/, has articles on colours and themes, fonts and maps, and on plot2() for users of ggplot2.
  • create_interactively() opens a Shiny app that builds a plot2() call from a point-and-click interface and shows the resulting code.
